title: Closing logomachy: both sides agree living faith includes trust and love
source_text: LXXI. Unde patet hic quoque multum esse logomachiae & verbalis contentionis. Nam dum Reformati plerique Theologi fiduciam & amorem ad fidem pertinere dicunt, & inter ejus actus numerari debere affirmant, fidem ut vivam considerant, & prout a fide mortua seu historica distinguitur: & asserunt fiduciam & dilectionem esse fidei actus, quoniam amor & fiducia, quae a fide viva separari non possunt, fidem vivam a mortua discriminant. Caeteroqui non negant, si quis in communi fidem definiat, & per illa tantum quae fidei tam mortuae, quam vivae competunt, hoc respectu nec amorem, nec fiduciam esse fidei partem, nec ejus ingredi definitionem. Et vice versa, dum Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae negant amorem atque fiduciam esse fidei actus, & fidem per amorem aut fiduciam esse definiendam, fidem ut saepius dictum est, considerant secundum id quod commune habet fidei tam mortuae, quam vivae. Si quis vero fidem vivam ut talem consideret, minime diffiteantur fiduciam & dilectionem ea includi, & tanquam actus ejus considerari posse.
pass_a_gloss: Whence it is clear that here too there is much logomachy and verbal contention. For when most Reformed theologians say that trust and love belong to faith and affirm they ought to be numbered among its acts, they consider faith as living and as distinguished from dead or historic faith; and they assert that trust and love are acts of faith because love and trust, which cannot be separated from living faith, discriminate living faith from dead. Otherwise they do not deny that if someone defines faith in common and only by those things that belong to dead as well as living faith, in that respect neither love nor trust is a part of faith or enters its definition. And conversely, when the Doctors of the Roman Church deny that love and trust are acts of faith and that faith is to be defined by love or trust, they consider faith, as has often been said, according to what it has in common with dead as well as living faith. But if anyone considers living faith as such, they by no means deny that trust and love are included in it and can be considered as its acts.
pass_b_english: Much of the fiducia/love fight is verbal: Reformed mean living faith as distinct from historic when they number trust and love among faith acts.

Rome denies those as acts of absolute faith common to dead and living, yet grants that living faith as such includes trust and love as its acts — so the Roman comparison block closes in shared substance.
